chapter_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 1 period = 40 minutes
Total: 1 periods · 40 minutes

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Activating Prior Knowledge and Meeting Krishtakka

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.1): word web — why literacy matters
Reflect and Respond (p.1): four oral prompts on grandparents and shared experiences

phases.description: Teacher introduces the chapter title and asks students to predict what the story might be about. Brief pair-share before anchoring the discussion.
Students individually complete the Reflect and Respond word web centred on why reading and writing matter. Two or three students share their webs aloud.

Class moves to Reflect and Respond oral prompts on grandparents' languages, shared time, favourite memories, and things elders enjoy watching youngsters do. Teacher facilitates a whole-class conversation, drawing out diverse family contexts.

Teacher reads the opening paragraph of the prose aloud (p.1), setting the scene of the Karnataka village, the delayed Karmaveera magazine, and the serialised Kashi Yatre novel. Students follow in their textbooks.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the chapter-opening period; no prior period to transition from. The story's north Karnataka village setting and the detail of delayed weekly magazines may need brief contextualising for urban students. The word web and oral prompts together warm up the theme of literacy and intergenerational relationships that run through the whole prose.
materials: Blackboard or chart for word web

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Reading for Meaning: Krishtakka's World and the Midnight Turning Point

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Meaning (p.2): match eight highlighted words to meanings
Check Your Understanding (p.6): cause-and-effect table for Part I

phases.description: Teacher-led shared reading of the passage on p.2 where the vocabulary matching task is embedded; students follow along and note the eight highlighted words in context before attempting the match.

Students individually match Reading for Meaning words (protagonist, debate, episode, community, concentration, eagerly, convincing, guided) with the boxed meanings. Answers are discussed as a class, with teacher highlighting how context clarifies meaning.
Shared reading continues through Part I (p.3–6), covering the narrator's departure to the wedding and the return to find Krishtakka weeping. Teacher pauses at key moments to question students.
Students work in pairs to complete the cause-and-effect table for Part I from Check Your Understanding (p.6). Pairs share one entry each; teacher consolidates on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Continues from the opening activation in Period 1. The cause-and-effect table is a comprehension scaffold; watch for students conflating cause and effect for the entry about Krishtakka's tears — the prose makes clear that the narrator's absence revealed Krishtakka's painful dependence, not merely the missed episode. The term 'Avva' (meaning 'mother' in north Karnataka Kannada) should be explained so students understand the tenderness of the grandmother-narrator bond.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Close Reading the Night-Terrace Scene and Krishtakka's Resolution

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.10–11): Extract 1 — five questions on the night-terrace scene
Critical Reflection (p.12): Extract 2 — five questions on grandmother's resolution

homework.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.12): did narrator expect grandmother's tears — short written response

phases.description: Teacher reads Part II aloud (p.7–10), covering the midnight terrace conversation, Krishtakka's declaration of independence, and the Dassara deadline. Students follow along noting stage-setting details.

Close reading of Extract 1 from Critical Reflection (p.10–11): the passage from Krishtakka's tears to her affectionate touch of the narrator's forehead. Students work through all five questions — multiple-choice, fill-in, and two extract-analysis items — in pairs, then share responses.

Close reading of Extract 2 from Critical Reflection (p.12): Krishtakka's statement 'I want to be independent' through the narrator's childish laughter. Students complete all five questions individually; class discussion follows, focusing on character inference and the narrator's assumptions about age and learning.

Teacher-led synthesis: how do both extracts together reveal Krishtakka's character arc from helplessness to determined agency? Students note one key insight in their exercise books. Homework is explained.

periods.teacher_notes: The two extracts are the analytical heart of the prose; budget the full 20 minutes each so no question is rushed. A common pitfall is treating the extract-analysis questions as recall — push students to quote specific phrases and explain their effect, as the prose makes Krishtakka's dignity and the narrator's initial condescension both visible in the language. Tasks on prediction (task 4) and how the narrator might help (task 5) are set as homework.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Critical Reflection: Extended Analysis and Theme Synthesis

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.12–13): seven extended-answer questions — theme, character, title justification

phases.description: Brief recap of homework responses (tasks 4 and 5). Teacher notes key ideas on the board and connects them to today's extended-answer focus.

Students read the seven extended-answer questions from Critical Reflection (p.12–13) silently, then in triads prioritise two they find most challenging. Teacher draws out which questions generated most uncertainty — typically the title-justification and effectiveness evaluation items.

Whole-class critical discussion: teacher facilitates responses to each of the seven questions in sequence, probing for evidence from the prose. Focus falls on the significance of Kashi Yatre as a parallel text, the grandmother's foot-touch as hierarchical reversal, and the broader theme of lifelong learning and independence.

Students independently write a four-to-six sentence response to the final question — how effectively the story highlights education as personal independence — in their exercise books. Two students share; teacher gives brief formative feedback.

periods.teacher_notes: Bridges from the extract work in Period 3 to synthesis-level thinking. The question about the significance of Kashi Yatre often prompts students to treat the embedded novel as mere plot device; guide them to see the structural parallel — the fictional old woman who chooses another's need over her own dream mirrors Krishtakka's earlier sacrifice of literacy. Tasks 5 and 6 (prediction and helping strategies) were set as homework in Period 3 and should surface organically in today's discussion.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Digital Literacy Listening and Turncoat Debate on Learning

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.17): five sentence-completion items on digital literacy talk
Speaking Activity (p.17): turncoat solo debate on two topics about language and age of learning

phases.description: Teacher explains the listening task format: students will hear a talk on digital literacy and fill in five sentence completions using one to three exact words. Sentences are read aloud once before the audio begins.

Teacher reads the transcript (p.259) at natural pace twice. Students complete the five Listen and Respond sentence-completion items (p.17) independently. Answers are verified together; teacher draws a quick thematic link between digital literacy and Krishtakka's literacy journey.

Teacher introduces the turncoat debate format: one minute for, then one minute against, with a clear switch signal. Sentence prompt cards are on the board. Students choose either Topic 1 (learning a new language) or Topic 2 (learning only when young) and prepare notes for both sides.

Four to six volunteers perform their turncoat debates before the class; teacher ensures both topics are covered. After each performance, brief whole-class feedback focuses on argument quality and smooth side-switching.
Teacher consolidates: which arguments were most convincing on each side? Students note one strong 'for' and one strong 'against' point in their books as a speaking-reflection prompt.

periods.teacher_notes: Transitions from the prose's reading-and-analysis work to oral skills. The digital literacy transcript (p.259) connects thematically to the chapter by broadening literacy from Kannada script to digital competence — make this link explicit to deepen engagement. In the turncoat debate, students often struggle to argue authentically for the side they personally disagree with; remind them that the skill is in marshalling evidence, not personal belief.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Letter to the Editor: Students as Adult Literacy Advocates

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.17): letter to editor on student participation in adult literacy camps

phases.description: Teacher models the formal letter format on the board — name/designation/address, date, subject line (four to five words), salutation, three-paragraph body plan, complimentary close — linking it to the Writing Task guidance on p.17.

Students plan their three body paragraphs in rough: paragraph one — importance of student participation; paragraph two — benefits for students and society; paragraph three — suggestions to spread awareness and recruit volunteers. Teacher circulates and prompts specificity.
Students draft the full letter in their exercise books, observing the format guidance. Teacher circulates, offering brief oral feedback on register (formal, clear, specific) and paragraph cohesion.
Two or three students read their letters aloud. Peer feedback focuses on one strength and one suggestion per letter, guided by the format checklist on the board.
Teacher summarises common strengths and a key pitfall — often the subject line is too vague. Students correct their subject lines before submitting.

periods.teacher_notes: Transitions from the speaking period to formal writing. The letter connects directly to the prose's theme: just as Krishtakka's narrator becomes her teacher, students are asked to imagine themselves as advocates for other adults' literacy. The most common weakness in student letters at this level is slipping into informal register in the body paragraphs; draw attention to phrases like 'I feel' versus 'It is strongly recommended'.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Binomials, Prefixes, and Idioms of Learning

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.13): match eight binomials, then use five in sentences
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.14): add prefixes to ten words from the column

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.15): match six learning idioms and use in sentences

phases.description: Teacher writes 'hide and seek' on the board and asks students where they encountered it in the prose. Introduces the term 'binomial' with one additional example ('back and forth').

Students match the eight binomials in Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.13) — sink or swim, on and off, mix and match, all or nothing, part and parcel, pick and choose, sooner or later, leaps and bounds — to their meanings, using a dictionary where needed. Five chosen binomials are then used in original sentences; two or three are shared.

Teacher draws attention to the prefix examples from the prose (unhappy, unusual, unfortunately, irrespective, independent). Students work through the ten prefix-formation items (p.14) — un, im, dis, in, mis, extra — and verify answers with a partner before whole-class check.
Teacher sets homework: the learning-idiom matching task (p.15) plus original sentences using all six idioms. Brief preview of the past-perfect grammar work coming in the next vocabulary period.

periods.teacher_notes: This is a dedicated vocabulary period; keep it distinct from grammar. Students often confuse 'in-' (negative: independent) with 'in-' (into: include) — take a minute to distinguish. Tasks 2 (ten prefix items) and 3 (five words from prose with prefix sentences) together constitute a natural progression; task 3 is left unanchored today given the period budget and can be used as an extension or self-study exercise.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Past Perfect vs Simple Past: Grammar in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.16): fill five sentence pairs — simple past vs past perfect
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.16): fill ten blanks in the financial-planning paragraph

phases.description: Teacher writes the two example sentences from the prose on the board — 'had been published' and 'had passed with flying colours' — and elicits the difference between simple past and past perfect using a timeline visual.

Students complete the five sentence-pair fill-in items (p.16) — sentences A through E using grammar-in-context scenarios. Pairs compare answers; teacher works through each, emphasising the sequence-of-events logic.

Students complete the ten-blank financial-planning paragraph (p.16), choosing between simple past and past perfect for each verb in brackets. Individual work, then full class verification with teacher highlighting items H–J where the distinction is subtle.
Quick consolidation: teacher asks students to write one original sentence using both tenses to describe something they had completed before a recent event. Two or three are shared.

periods.teacher_notes: Continues from the vocabulary period in Period 7; no gap in the grammar sequence. The financial-planning paragraph is a deliberately contemporary context; connect it briefly to the digital literacy listening text from Period 5 to reinforce cross-text vocabulary. Students frequently over-apply past perfect — stress that it is only needed when two past events must be sequenced relative to each other.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Kinship Terms Across Indian Languages and Literacy Missions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.21): complete kinship-terms table in five Indian languages

homework.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.21–22): gift a favourite book or magazine to a grandparent

phases.description: Teacher recaps the word 'Avva' from the prose and its north Karnataka Kannada meaning. Asks: how many students know the word for grandmother in their home language? Quick show of hands across the class.

Students, in groups of four, complete the kinship-terms table (p.21) for at least five Indian languages — using Kannada as the model row already filled in. Each group covers different language families (Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Tibeto-Burman, Austroasiatic). Groups share their completed rows; teacher builds a master table on the board.

Teacher leads a brief reading and discussion of the 'Do you know?' informational passages (p.21–22) covering the National Literacy Mission Authority, financial literacy, the Early Literacy Project, and the CCRT. Students identify one fact from each passage that surprises them.
Teacher sets the grandparent-gift homework (p.21–22 task 3). Students briefly discuss in pairs which book or magazine they would choose and why, before noting it in their diaries.

periods.teacher_notes: This closes Section A and moves into a multilingual, cultural-heritage mode that previews the poem's celebration of India's diversity. The kinship-terms activity often surfaces students' pride in regional languages; allow space for this. The 'Do you know?' passages are informational and do not require deep analysis — a brisk read and one-fact-per-passage response keeps the pace without overloading. Task 2 (four informational 'Do you know?' project items) is partially covered in class reading; full independent research is unanchored and noted here as a self-study pointer.

periods.activity_title: Reading the Ode Aloud and Unpacking Symbols and Devices

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.23): complete National Anthem table — states, mountains, rivers
Check Your Understanding (p.23): odd-one-out for four underlined words

phases.description: Teacher introduces Section B: the poem 'Bharat Our Land', translated from Subramania Bharati's Tamil original. Brief context — Bharati as a Tamil poet-patriot, the poem as a patriotic ode. Teacher reads the full poem aloud expressively; students follow in their textbooks (p.23–24).

Students recall lines of the National Anthem and complete the Reflect and Respond table (p.23) listing states, mountain ranges, and rivers mentioned in it. Pair verification, then brief class discussion linking the Anthem's geography to Bharati's imagery.

Students read the four odd-one-out items (Check Your Understanding, p.23) — peerless, sanctified, auspicious, hoary antiquity — working individually then discussing with a neighbour. Class consolidation: teacher explains how contextual meaning eliminates the outlier in each set.

Teacher introduces the concepts of ode, refrain, apostrophe, allusion, and hyperbole using the poem's own lines as examples. Students annotate their poem text with device labels for at least one example of each.

periods.teacher_notes: Transitions from Section A's prose world to a short patriotic poem; the thematic link is India's heritage of knowledge and sages, which parallels the prose's celebration of literacy. The terms 'Himavant', 'Upanishads', 'Brahma-knowledge', and 'dhamma' may be unfamiliar to students outside certain cultural backgrounds — give one-line explanations rather than extended lectures. The poem's second Reflect and Respond task (task 1, 'Jaya he' pair discussion) is left unanchored given the period budget; it can serve as a brief warm-up or self-study.

periods.activity_title: Deep Reading: Extract Analysis, Imagery, and Critical Reflection

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.28–29): Extract — five questions on Himavant–Ganga–Upanishads stanza
Critical Reflection (p.29): five extended-answer questions on cultural identity and national pride

phases.description: Quick review of device labels from Period 10 annotations. Teacher reads the first stanza aloud again, asking students to notice the effect of the hyphens before moving into the extract.

Students work through all five questions in the Critical Reflection extract on the Himavant–Ganga–Upanishads stanza (p.28–29): fill-in, multiple-choice, and two short-answer items. Answers discussed as a class with attention to how the rhetorical questions and the word 'generous' carry argumentative weight.

Students select three of the five extended-answer questions (p.29) to answer in writing in their exercise books. Teacher circulates; then two or three responses are shared for peer and teacher feedback focusing on textual evidence.
Teacher previews Period 12: vocabulary and beyond-text work on the poem. Students note one unanswered question from today's discussion to bring to the next class.

periods.teacher_notes: Continues the literary-analysis work begun in Period 10. The extended-answer questions here are richer than the prose's — they require connecting specific devices (refrain, hyperbole, allusion) to patriotic effect. Students often answer the 'national pride' question superficially; push them to name the specific poetic choice (e.g., the chant-like refrain) that creates the effect rather than paraphrasing the content.

periods.activity_title: Suffix Building, Patriotic Songs Across Languages, and India's Geographies

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary in Context (p.29): find poem words for four suffixes in the table
Learning Beyond the Text (p.31–32): find patriotic poems or songs in regional language and explain meaning

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary in Context (p.30): add four suffixes (-tion, -ive, -ment, -ed) to form new words and write sentences

phases.description: Teacher recaps the poem's key vocabulary. Introduces the suffix activity: what endings do 'generous', 'auspicious', 'antiquity', and 'peerless' share? Students identify the four suffixes (-ous, -ity, -est, -less) before opening the table.

Students complete the Vocabulary in Context suffix table (p.29) by locating poem words for each of the four suffixes. Class verification; teacher notes the morphological patterns on the board and asks students to generate one additional word per suffix from outside the poem.
Teacher sets suffix sentence-building as homework (p.30, four suffixes) and explains the task clearly. Students note the homework in their diaries.

Students, in groups of three, share a patriotic poem or song they know in their regional language — or one they locate via the textbook's cue (p.31–32). Each group presents a two-minute explanation of meaning and feeling to the class. Teacher facilitates connections between regional expressions of patriotism and Bharati's Tamil ode.

Teacher previews the interdisciplinary project on India's geographical features (p.31–32, task 2) as a self-study and group project for the coming weeks, explaining the six features and the expectation of linking region, importance, and language. Chapter wrap-up: students name one idea from Section A and one from Section B that they will carry forward.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing period integrates vocabulary and multilingual beyond-text work, bringing the chapter full circle — from one grandmother's Kannada literacy to India's many-languaged cultural heritage. The interdisciplinary geography project (p.31–32, task 2) is not anchored in this period due to time; it is flagged here as a self-study and group project pointer. The speaking and listening activities for Section B (oral cues on hometown pride; listening to four travellers) are unanchored given Section B's one-period share; they are noted as suitable self-study or homework extension tasks.
